text: What's going on in Psalm 82 and why did
Jesus quote it? Hey everybody, I'm Dan
Mlelen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and
religion. And Psalm 82 is one of the
Psalms of ASF. It is a very short psalm,
only eight verses long, but it is very
controversial and mythological. It talks
about God taking their stand within the
divine council or the council of L and
then judging the other members of the
council culminating in their
condemnation to mortality. And then in
the very last verse we have the psalmist
calling upon God to rise up and inherit
all nations. Now what's going on here? A
lot of scholars think that this is a
very archaic psalm and it may even
reflect a distinction between the most
high Elon who's identified as L and
Adoni. For instance, God is called upon
to rise up indicating they've been
seated but the deity who is talking
throughout the majority of the psalm
takes their stand in the divine council.
There are other folks who think that
Elohim refers to humans and so this is
about corrupt judges for instance. But
this is rejected by the overwhelming
majority of critical scholars. I have
written a paper on this that was
published in the journal of biblical
literature in 2018 entitled the God's
complaint psalm 82 as a psalm of
complaint. And what I argue there is
that this is the God of Israel standing
up to condemn the other gods of the
nations who are the other members of the
divine council for their negligence
regarding cosmic and social order and
justice. And what did they do to neglect
their duties related to cosmic and
social order and justice? They allowed
Babylon to invade Israel and cart off
the Israelites or more accurately the
Judahites into exile. This is what
allowed the foundations of the earth to
be rocked. And so God, the God of
Israel, is standing up to condemn them
and refers to them as gods and children
of the most high, but then condemns them
to mortality. Says, "You shall die like
men and fall like any prince." And what
this does is deposes them from their
seats on the divine council. Now those
seats sit empty. And this is when the
psalmist says, "Rise up, oh God, and
judge the earth. You inherit all
nations." And this is a call back to
Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where Adonai
receives as their inheritance, their
share of the inheritance, the nation of
Israel. And Israel is referred to as
Adonai's inheritance in a few different
places in the Hebrew Bible. But the idea
here is that now Adonai's purview, their
sovereignty can extend beyond the nation
of Israel. They will inherit all nations
by taking over all of the seats on the
divine council and in effect becoming
the patron deity of all nations of the
earth. And this I argue in my paper
affects
the universalization of Adonai's
geopolitical sovereignty. Prior to the
exile, Adonai's sovereignty on earth,
not in heaven, on earth was limited to
the land of Israel. This is why non for
instance when he goes back to Syria,
wants to worship Adonai in Syria, has to
bring two cartloads of Israelite soil
with him because Adonai can only be
worshiped on Israelite soil. And lest
someone say, "Well, that's a
non-Israelite. That's a pagan
perspective." It's also David's
perspective because when Saul is chasing
David, at one point he yells at Saul and
says, "Your men are forcing me out of
Adonai's inheritance, telling me, go
worship other gods." The idea there is
clearly that David cannot worship Adonai
if he has been forced out of Adonai's
inheritance, the land of Israel. He must
worship whatever deity is sovereign on
the soil on which he is. And we see this
reflected in the laments about the exile
where the Judahites sit on the bank of
the river in Babylon and say, "How can
we sing the song of Adonai in a foreign
land?" And so what Psalm 82 is doing in
a post- exilic context is expanding
Adonai's sovereignty to make Adonai
accessible to the Judahites who are
still living outside the land of Israel.
It universalizes Adonai. And there are
different ways that different authors
are trying to do that. Deuteria is
trying to do that. Ezekiel is trying to
do that. There are a variety of
different rhetorical attempts to expand
Adonai's sovereignty. So that's what I
argue Psalm 82 is about and that fits
broadly within the critical scholarly
consensus that this is a psalm that
takes place in a heavenly courtroom that
involves the divine council and I date
it a little later than most scholars
because I don't think that it is
distinguishing Adoni and L and I think
it is about Adonai's universalization in
the post- exilic period. But why would
Jesus quote this psalm in John 10:es
Well, couple things to note here. The
first thing is that the interpretation
of the psalm had changed by the first
century CE. They no longer had the same
worldview that they had in the sixth or
fifth centuries BCE. And they're on the
other side of the Greco Roman period and
they're reinterpreting things. And one
of the most popular interpretations of
Psalm 82 that we see in the early
rabbitic literature is the understanding
of Psalm 82 as having to do with the
reception of the law of Moses on Mount
Si. The idea there was that the people
of Israel are the ones being condemned.
And the people of Israel upon reception
of the law at Mount Si became freed from
the power of the angel of death. in
effect became immortal which rendered
them gods. And so when they sin with the
golden calf, that's what brings up Psalm
82. That is where God condemns them.
Says, "You are gods and children of the
most high in virtue of having received
the law, but you shall die like men and
fall like any prince." That is the
outcome of their sin with the golden
calf. They're condemned back down to
mortality. And I think, and there are a
lot of scholars who agree with me, that
what's going on here is the author of
the Gospel of John understands Psalm 82
in that way. And so is going to have
Jesus understand it in that way as well.
And in John 10, Jesus says, "I and the
father are one." And this is not the
Trinity. This is not Jesus saying, "I am
God." It's Jesus saying, "I and God have
a mutual inddwelling." And this mutual
inddwelling, Jesus' praise will be
extended, expanded to his own followers
in John 17. And in John 10, when his
accusers say, "How can you say that?
You're just a human and you're making
yourself divine." Jesus quotes Psalm 82,
talking about how the folks to whom the
word of God came, that would be the law
of Moses, were called gods in the
scriptures. And this is Psalm 82:6. You
are gods and children of the most high.
And so he's saying you cannot deny the
scriptures reference to these people as
gods and as children of the most high.
So why are you getting on my case when I
say I am the son of God? And the idea
there is that participation in divinity
can render someone divine. Now Jesus is
not saying I am divine by virtue of
reception of the word. Jesus is claiming
to be the very word itself. But Jesus is
using this passage to indicate there is
nothing inappropriate about him
identifying as the son of God. There is
nothing blasphemous about saying that in
light of the fact that the scriptures
refer to other humans as gods and as
sons of Elon, sons of the most high
because they have received the word of
God. This is the very word itself
standing before them. And so it's not
blasphemous for him to identify as the
son of God. So the author of John 10 is
having Jesus interpret Psalm 82
according to a later Greco Roman and
rabbitic Jewish interpretation that
understands the gods to be the
Israelites at Mount Si upon reception of
the law of Moses. So in that sense we
have two different ways of understanding
Psalm 82. the way the authors and
earliest audiences most likely
understood it and the way it was
understood in the first century CE and
later. And these understandings are very
different. But that's what's going on in
Psalm 82. And that's most likely why
Jesus is represented in the Gospel of
John as quoting Psalm 82, appealing to
the scriptures references to humans as
becoming gods in defense of his own
identification as the son of God. And
